Whether passive takings will serve this role effectively depends significantly on what it means for the government to render people more vulnerable to harm. The constitutional origins of this inquiry in DeShaney invoked federal prisoners and those in the custody of the state. In its most limited form, the duty to act arises when the State by the affirmative exercise of its power so restrains an individual s liberty that it renders him unable to care for himself, and at the same time fails to provide for his basic human needs . . . . 131 Or, more broadly, the State may be obligated to act when it is aware of the  [*1444]  dangers faced in the free world, and renders someone more vulnerable to them. 132
